column5: Tonight, I turn Chicago back on.
And it's the last thing I'll ever do.
I'm Mark. Night supervisor. City Grid Control.
Eight days ago, something got into the wires. So I shut the city off.
Last night, the man from the radio looked at me. His eyes were lit.
You know the code, Mark. Turn us back on.
His hand closed on my wrist. Hot. Humming.
Then a flare hit the street.
The woman in the gray coat.
Run! Don't let him take the badge!
We ran until the trucks were just noise behind us.
Under a dead streetlight, she finally told me her name.
Dana. Day shift. I sat next to you for six years.
On day one, the current went through you. It burned your memory out.
So I wrote in your notebook. Every night. So you'd remember what we did.
I asked her where the people on my list went.
She pointed north.
One place in the whole city still had light.
Wrigley Field. Running on its own generators.
Forty thousand people in the stands.
Not moving. Every pair of eyes, lit.
It never starved, Mark. It's been keeping them.
It needs your code to get into every house at once.
So I gave it what it wanted.
Every volt in Chicago. All of it. Into one line.
Straight into Wrigley.
The control room was cold. My chair still pushed in.
I typed the code. Zero. Nine. One. Four.
Mark. Don't. We are your city.
I pulled the breaker.
And I didn't let go.
The lights came back on. Block by block. Starting with the north side.
At Wrigley, forty thousand people blinked.
Normal eyes.
Mrs. Alvarez's grandson walked home that morning.
Dana found my notebook on the control room floor.
One last line. In my handwriting.
If your lights ever flicker three times, don't be scared.
It's just me. Still checking names off the list.
